For an arbitrary number of users, we derive the input-output quadrature relations describing the multiuser q-CDMA CV-QKD system. Using this model, we evaluate the achievable secret key rate under collective attacks with reverse reconciliation. We further investigate the impact of key system parameters including the correction factor, multiuser interference noise, environmental noise, and channel transmittance. A comparison between the asymptotic and finite-size regimes is also presented to highlight the associated performance trade-offs. These results provide a theoretical framework for assessing the performance of q-CDMA-based CV-QKD and support the development of scalable and secure multiuser quantum communication networks.

AI.tldr: Quantum CDMA framework for multiuser CV-QKD using chaotic phase encoding for secure multiplexed quantum communication.
AI.motivation: To develop a scalable multiuser quantum communication system that enables multiple users to share a quantum channel securely for continuous-variable quantum key distribution.
AI.method: Uses chaotic phase shifters for encoding/decoding quantum states, beam splitter networks for multiplexing/demultiplexing, synchronized chaotic systems for reliable state recovery, and derives input-output quadrature relations for arbitrary number of users.
AI.result: Derived achievable secret key rates under collective attacks with reverse reconciliation, analyzed impact of system parameters (correction factor, multiuser interference, environmental noise, channel transmittance), and compared asymptotic vs finite-size regimes.
AI.conclusion: Provides theoretical framework for q-CDMA-based CV-QKD performance assessment, supporting development of scalable, secure multiuser quantum communication networks.

title: A Directly Modulated Laser Platform for High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution
summary: High-dimensional quantum key distribution (HD-QKD) offers a promising approach to enhance secret key rates beyond conventional binary-encoded QKD, addressing the growing demand for secure data transmission. However, the practical application of most HD-QKD systems has been hindered by their complexity, as they require the preparation and detection of quantum states in large Hilbert spaces. Here, we design and experimentally realize a directly modulated laser platform for HD-QKD. It operates at a repetition rate of 312.5 MHz, yielding a remarkably simple and scalable architecture. Through which, we achieve a record transmission distance of 250 km for HD-QKD, demonstrating its feasibility for long-distance quantum communication. Furthermore, we witness that the four-dimensional states outperform their two-dimensional counterpart in secret key rate, highlighting the practical advantage of high-dimensional encoding. This simple and scalable approach shows strong potential for chip-scale integration.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of a simple, directly modulated laser platform for high-dimensional quantum key distribution achieving record 250 km transmission distance with 312.5 MHz repetition rate.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional QKD promises higher secret key rates than binary QKD, but practical implementation has been hindered by complexity requiring preparation/detection in large Hilbert spaces.
AI.method: Design and experimental realization of a directly modulated laser platform for HD-QKD operating at 312.5 MHz repetition rate, creating a simple and scalable architecture.
AI.result: Achieved record 250 km transmission distance for HD-QKD, with four-dimensional states outperforming two-dimensional counterparts in secret key rate, demonstrating practical advantage of high-dimensional encoding.
AI.conclusion: The simple and scalable approach shows strong potential for chip-scale integration and demonstrates feasibility for long-distance quantum communication using high-dimensional encoding.

title: Deep-Learning-Designed AlGaAs Interface Linking Trapped Ions to Telecom Quantum Networks
summary: The realization of a scalable quantum internet requires efficient light-matter interfaces that map stationary qubits onto photonic carriers for long-distance transmission. A central challenge is the generation of entangled photons simultaneously compatible with single-emitter transitions and low-loss telecom fiber infrastructure. Spontaneous parametric down-conversion in integrated photonic platforms offers a promising route toward this goal. Among available material systems, AlGaAs is particularly attractive due to its large second-order nonlinearity and strong potential for monolithic integration. However, engineering the spectral and spatial properties of the generated quantum states requires the simultaneous optimization of numerous geometric and material parameters, a task remaining computationally demanding for conventional numerical approaches. To address this challenge and enable rapid and high-fidelity modeling of complex nonlinear photonic devices, we develop an inverse-design framework based on neural network surrogate models. Using this readily extendable method, we design a transversely pumped AlGaAs waveguide microcavity that produces polarization-entangled photon pairs in distinct spatial modes and frequency channels, one at 1092 nm, resonant with a $^{88}\text{Sr}^{+}$ transition, and the other at 1550 nm in the telecom C-band. This device establishes a direct photonic interface between trapped-ion qubits and long-haul fiber networks, providing a scalable pathway toward hybrid quantum network architectures.

AI.tldr: Neural network inverse design enables AlGaAs waveguide microcavity generating polarization-entangled photon pairs at 1092 nm (Sr+ ion transition) and 1550 nm (telecom C-band) for hybrid quantum networks.
AI.motivation: Need efficient light-matter interfaces for quantum internet that generate entangled photons compatible with single-emitter transitions and telecom fiber infrastructure, overcoming computational challenges in optimizing complex nonlinear photonic devices.
AI.method: Develop inverse-design framework using neural network surrogate models to rapidly optimize AlGaAs waveguide microcavity parameters, enabling design of transversely pumped device producing polarization-entangled photon pairs via spontaneous parametric down-conversion.
AI.result: Designed AlGaAs waveguide microcavity generates polarization-entangled photon pairs in distinct spatial modes and frequency channels: one at 1092 nm (resonant with Sr+ ion transition) and one at 1550 nm (telecom C-band).
AI.conclusion: The device establishes direct photonic interface between trapped-ion qubits and long-haul fiber networks, providing scalable pathway toward hybrid quantum network architectures using neural network inverse design.

title: Auger Spectroscopy via Generative Quantum Eigensolver: A Quantum Approach to Molecular Excitations
summary: Auger electron spectroscopy, a way of characterizing electronic structure through core-level decay processes, is widely used in materials characterization; however direct calculation from molecular geometry requires accurate treatment of many excited states, posing a challenge for classical methods. We present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow for calculating Auger spectra that combines the generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) for ground-state preparation, the quantum self-consistent equation-of-motion method for excited-state calculations, and the one-centre approximation for Auger transition rates. GQE uses a GPT-2 model to generate quantum circuits for ground-state optimization, allowing our workflow to benefit from HPC parallelization and GPU-acceleration for favourable scaling with system size. We demonstrate the validity of our workflow by calculating the Auger spectrum of water with the STO-3G basis set and demonstrating qualitative and quantitative agreement with spectra obtained using completely classical full configuration interaction calculations, from the computational literature, and from the experimental literature. We also find that for water, substituting the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for GQE results in near-identical spectra, but that the ground state estimator generated by GQE contains about half the total gate count as that generated by VQE.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum-classical workflow using generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) for calculating Auger spectra with reduced circuit complexity compared to VQE.
AI.motivation: Direct calculation of Auger spectra from molecular geometry requires accurate treatment of many excited states, which is challenging for classical methods. Quantum computing offers potential advantages but faces circuit complexity issues with traditional variational approaches.
AI.method: Hybrid workflow combining: 1) Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) using GPT-2 model to generate quantum circuits for ground-state preparation, 2) Quantum self-consistent equation-of-motion method for excited-state calculations, and 3) One-centre approximation for Auger transition rates. The approach leverages HPC parallelization and GPU acceleration.
AI.result: Demonstrated validity by calculating water's Auger spectrum with STO-3G basis, showing qualitative and quantitative agreement with classical full configuration interaction calculations, computational literature, and experimental data. GQE produced ground state estimator with about half the total gate count compared to VQE while yielding near-identical spectra.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid quantum-classical workflow successfully calculates Auger spectra with reduced quantum circuit complexity, demonstrating the potential of generative approaches like GQE to overcome scalability limitations of traditional variational quantum algorithms for excited-state spectroscopy.

title: Nonlocal continuous-variable quantum nondemolition gates by optical connections
summary: Nonlocal quantum gates, coupling quantum systems located at distance, are crucial for distributed quantum computing. High-capacity optical noiseless connections between these quantum systems are essential for transmitting large amounts of information per mode. We propose a library of feasible protocols to implement a necessary nonlocal continuous-variable (CV) quantum nondemolition (QND) gate between two distant users sharing a quantum channel with a newly available element - single-pass phase-sensitive optical parametric amplifiers (OPAs), allowing for both online squeezing and channel-loss compensation, and classical communication between them. The use of OPAs enhances quality of the resulting entangling gate in terms of both excess noise and logarithmic negativity. The proposed schemes are also applicable to CV cluster state fusion, providing a first step towards development of distributed CV measurement-based quantum computation.

AI.tldr: Protocols for implementing nonlocal continuous-variable quantum nondemolition gates between distant users using phase-sensitive optical parametric amplifiers for enhanced entanglement quality and distributed quantum computing applications.
AI.motivation: Nonlocal quantum gates are essential for distributed quantum computing, requiring high-capacity optical connections between distant quantum systems to transmit large amounts of information per mode.
AI.method: Proposes a library of feasible protocols using single-pass phase-sensitive optical parametric amplifiers (OPAs) that enable both online squeezing and channel-loss compensation, combined with classical communication between distant users sharing a quantum channel.
AI.result: OPAs enhance the quality of the resulting entangling gate in terms of both excess noise reduction and increased logarithmic negativity (entanglement measure).
AI.conclusion: The proposed schemes are applicable to continuous-variable cluster state fusion, providing a foundational step toward developing distributed CV measurement-based quantum computation.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Quantum Circuits for Comparators and Incrementers
summary: We present quantum circuits for comparison and increment operations that achieve an asymptotically optimal gate count of $Θ(n)$ and depth of $Θ(\log n)$ over the Clifford+Toffoli gate set, while using a provably minimal number of qubits. We extend these results to classical-quantum comparators, yielding an improved classical-quantum adder with an optimal qubit count. Given the ubiquity of these operations as algorithmic building blocks, our constructions translate directly into reduced circuit complexity for many quantum algorithms. As a notable example, they can be used to improve a space-efficient circuit for Shor's factoring algorithm, reducing circuit depth from $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ to $\mathcal{O}(n^2 \log^2 n)$ without increasing either the qubit count or the asymptotic gate complexity. Underpinning these results is a general theorem demonstrating how to trade ancilla qubits for control qubits with low overhead in both depth and gate count, providing a broadly applicable tool for quantum circuit design.

AI.tldr: Quantum circuits for comparison and increment operations achieve optimal gate count Θ(n) and depth Θ(log n) with minimal qubits, improving Shor's algorithm depth from O(n³) to O(n² log² n).
AI.motivation: Comparison and increment operations are fundamental building blocks in quantum algorithms, but existing implementations often use excessive resources. There is a need for asymptotically optimal circuits that minimize both gate count, depth, and qubit usage to improve overall quantum algorithm efficiency.
AI.method: Develop quantum circuits for comparison and increment operations over Clifford+Toffoli gate set, achieving optimal gate count and depth with provably minimal qubits. Extend to classical-quantum comparators for improved adder design. Use a general theorem to trade ancilla qubits for control qubits with low overhead.
AI.result: Achieved asymptotically optimal gate count Θ(n) and depth Θ(log n) for comparison/increment operations with minimal qubits. Improved classical-quantum adder with optimal qubit count. Reduced Shor's factoring algorithm circuit depth from O(n³) to O(n² log² n) without increasing qubit count or asymptotic gate complexity.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents resource-optimal quantum circuits for fundamental operations, providing broadly applicable tools for quantum circuit design. The general theorem for trading ancilla qubits for control qubits enables significant improvements in quantum algorithm complexity, particularly demonstrated for Shor's factoring algorithm.

title: Inaccurate (weak) measurements classical and quantum
summary: We consider highly inaccurate measurements made on classical stochastic and quantum systems. In the quantum case such a \e{weak} measurement preserves coherence between the system's alternatives. We demonstrate that in both cases the information about the scenario realised in each individual trial is lost. However, ensemble parameters such as classical path probabilities, and quantum quasi-probabilities can be extracted from the obtained statistics. In both cases causality ensures that additional post-selection only redistributes individual outcomes between the system's final states. Quantum quasi-probabilities may change sign, which allows for anomalously large meter's (pointer's) reading for some final states. These, we show, result from mere \e{reshaping} of a broad distribution obtained earlier, and provide no \e{experimental evidence} of quantum variables taking, on rare occasions, exceptionally large values.

AI.tldr: Weak measurements on classical and quantum systems lose individual trial information but allow extraction of ensemble parameters like path probabilities and quantum quasi-probabilities, with quantum negativity enabling anomalously large meter readings through distribution reshaping rather than actual large quantum values.
AI.motivation: To understand how weak (highly inaccurate) measurements affect information extraction from both classical stochastic and quantum systems, particularly examining what information is preserved or lost and how quantum quasi-probabilities differ from classical probabilities.
AI.method: Analysis of weak measurements that preserve quantum coherence, comparison of classical and quantum cases, examination of causality constraints, and investigation of post-selection effects on outcome distributions.
AI.result: Weak measurements lose information about individual trial scenarios but allow extraction of ensemble parameters; quantum quasi-probabilities can be negative, enabling anomalously large meter readings through distribution reshaping rather than actual large quantum values.
AI.conclusion: Anomalously large meter readings in quantum weak measurements result from distribution reshaping due to negative quasi-probabilities, not from quantum variables taking exceptionally large values, challenging naive interpretations of weak measurement results.

title: Fast Arbitrary Qutrit Gates for NV Centers in the Low-Field Regime
summary: The ground state of the negatively charged NV center forms a spin-1 manifold providing a versatile platform for sensing and information processing. Here we present a scheme for implementing fast arbitrary qutrit gates in the low-field regime using monochromatic microwave pulses of constant intensity tuned to the zero-field transition. By concatenating pulses with appropriate phases and durations, the NV-ERC scheme is extended from SU(2) operations in the double-quantum subspace to the full three-level structure. We show that arbitrary SU(3) operations can be decomposed into rotations in the double-quantum subspace together with effective implementations of the generators related to $\hatλ_5$ and $\hatλ_8$. We illustrate this decomposition with a use case: performing quantum state tomography of the complete three-level density matrix.

AI.tldr: Fast arbitrary qutrit gates for NV centers using monochromatic microwave pulses tuned to zero-field transition, enabling full SU(3) operations and quantum state tomography.
AI.motivation: The negatively charged NV center's spin-1 manifold provides a versatile platform for quantum sensing and information processing, but efficient implementation of arbitrary qutrit gates in the full three-level structure is needed.
AI.method: Extend the NV-ERC scheme from SU(2) operations in the double-quantum subspace to full three-level structure using monochromatic microwave pulses of constant intensity tuned to the zero-field transition. Concatenate pulses with appropriate phases and durations, decomposing arbitrary SU(3) operations into rotations in the double-quantum subspace plus effective implementations of generators related to λ̂₅ and λ̂₈.
AI.result: Demonstrated scheme for implementing fast arbitrary qutrit gates in the low-field regime, enabling complete quantum state tomography of the three-level density matrix as a use case.
AI.conclusion: The presented scheme provides a practical method for implementing arbitrary SU(3) operations on NV center qutrits using microwave control, expanding quantum information processing capabilities beyond qubit operations to full qutrit manipulation.

title: Breaking concentration barriers for quantum extreme learning on digital quantum processors
summary: Reservoir computing leverages rich, non-linear dynamics to process temporal data. Quantum variants promise enhanced expressivity from high-dimensional Hilbert spaces, yet their practical applicability is hindered by hardware noise and concentration effects that can erase input-output distinguishability at large system sizes. In this work, we present and experimentally demonstrate a Quantum Extreme Learning Machine (QELM) tailored to state-of-the-art superconducting platforms, employing up to 124 qubits and circuits with more than 5,000 two-qubit gates on IBM Quantum computers. We introduce a practical multi-objective hyperparameter tuning strategy that jointly monitors observable variability, capacity, and task performance to identify noise-robust operating points. In addition, we develop a local eigentask analysis that enables computationally efficient feature selection and effective information retrieval. We report evidence of a regime of optimality that is identifiable at small scales and transferable across tasks and larger systems, and we achieve performances competitive with leading classical baselines on representative benchmarks for time-series forecasting and satellite image classification. Together, our results establish a viable and robust framework for large-scale, pre-fault-tolerant quantum machine learning and provide a foundation for extending reservoir-based methods to more expressive architectures and real-world scenarios.

AI.tldr: QELM framework for large-scale quantum reservoir computing on noisy hardware achieves competitive performance on time-series and image tasks through noise-robust hyperparameter tuning and local eigentask analysis.
AI.motivation: Quantum reservoir computing offers enhanced expressivity but faces practical limitations from hardware noise and concentration effects that erase input-output distinguishability at large scales.
AI.method: Developed Quantum Extreme Learning Machine (QELM) for superconducting platforms using up to 124 qubits; introduced multi-objective hyperparameter tuning monitoring observable variability, capacity, and task performance; created local eigentask analysis for efficient feature selection.
AI.result: Achieved competitive performance with classical baselines on time-series forecasting and satellite image classification; identified transferable optimality regime identifiable at small scales; demonstrated viability on IBM Quantum computers with circuits exceeding 5,000 two-qubit gates.
AI.conclusion: Establishes robust framework for large-scale, pre-fault-tolerant quantum machine learning; provides foundation for extending reservoir-based methods to more expressive architectures and real-world applications.

title: Quantum timekeeping and the dynamics of scrambling in critical systems
summary: In this work, we develop a quantum metrological framework for quantum chaos by showing that local subsystems of information scrambling systems naturally function as quantum stopwatches. The reduced quantum state of a subsystem encodes the passage of time through its growing distinguishability from the initial preparation. Treating time as the estimation parameter, we then derive a generalized quantum Cramer-Rao bound that directly relates the precision of time estimation to the decay of out-of-time ordered correlators (OTOCs) and subsystem quantum Fisher information (QFI). As a main result, we obtain continuity bounds for quantum Lyapunov exponent in terms of the subsystem QFI in quantumly chaotic dynamics. Furthermore, using a scaling analysis based on imaginary-time correlators, we show that the subsystem QFI exhibits universal critical amplification near quantum phase transitions. Our results are demonstrated and verified by a numerical analysis of the dynamics of a chaotic Ising chain.

AI.tldr: Quantum chaos framework uses local subsystems as quantum stopwatches, relating time estimation precision to OTOC decay and subsystem quantum Fisher information, with applications to Lyapunov exponents and quantum phase transitions.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum metrological framework for quantum chaos by showing that local subsystems of information scrambling systems can function as quantum stopwatches, enabling time estimation through subsystem distinguishability.
AI.method: Treat time as estimation parameter, derive generalized quantum Cramer-Rao bound relating time estimation precision to OTOC decay and subsystem quantum Fisher information (QFI), obtain continuity bounds for quantum Lyapunov exponents, use scaling analysis with imaginary-time correlators to show universal critical amplification near quantum phase transitions, and verify with numerical analysis of chaotic Ising chain dynamics.
AI.result: Local subsystems encode time through growing distinguishability from initial state; derived relation between time estimation precision and OTOC decay/QFI; obtained continuity bounds for quantum Lyapunov exponents in terms of subsystem QFI; demonstrated universal critical amplification of subsystem QFI near quantum phase transitions; verified with chaotic Ising chain simulations.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes local subsystems as quantum stopwatches in chaotic systems, provides fundamental connections between quantum metrology, information scrambling, and chaos through OTOC-QFI relations, and reveals universal critical behavior near quantum phase transitions with implications for quantum sensing and characterization of quantum chaotic dynamics.

title: Structured Quantum Optimal Control under Bandwidth and Smoothness Constraints-An Inexact Proximal-ADMM Approach for Low-Complexity Pulse Synthesis
summary: Quantum optimal control is often judged by nominal fidelity alone, even though realistic pulse-design studies must also account for bandwidth, amplitude, and smoothness constraints. I study this structured-control regime with an inexact Proximal-ADMM framework that combines gate-infidelity minimization with $L_1$ sparsity, total-variation regularization, explicit band-limit projection, and box constraints in a single loop. The method is benchmarked against GRAPE, standard Krotov, and L-BFGS-B on a single-qubit $X$ gate, a leakage-prone qutrit task, and a two-qubit entangling gate. Across ten random seeds, Pareto scans, ablations, filtered-baseline fairness checks, significance analysis with false-discovery-rate correction, and robustness tests, the method is not a universal winner in either nominal fidelity or wall-clock cost. Its value is instead to expose and stabilize a low-complexity frontier of the fidelity-complexity landscape. After retuning the PADMM budgets and warm-start lengths, the qutrit and two-qubit structured fidelities rise to 0.6672 +- 0.0001 and 0.6342 +- 0.0003, respectively, while preserving markedly lower complexity than unconstrained quasi-Newton solutions. These values remain well below deployment-grade gate thresholds, so the contribution should still be read as a numerical framework for constrained pulse synthesis rather than as a finished route to immediately deployable high-fidelity gates. Training-time robust optimization yields only task-dependent gains, with the clearest effect appearing in qutrit drift robustness and amounting to a small absolute improvement. The results therefore position PADMM as a constraint-native framework for low-complexity frontier exploration, not as a replacement for unconstrained high-fidelity solvers.

AI.tldr: Proximal-ADMM framework for quantum optimal control with multiple constraints (sparsity, TV regularization, band-limit, box constraints) benchmarked against standard methods, showing value in exploring low-complexity frontier rather than achieving highest fidelities.
AI.motivation: Quantum optimal control typically focuses on nominal fidelity alone, but realistic pulse design requires handling multiple constraints including bandwidth, amplitude, smoothness, and sparsity simultaneously.
AI.method: Inexact Proximal-ADMM framework combining gate-infidelity minimization with L1 sparsity, total-variation regularization, explicit band-limit projection, and box constraints in a single optimization loop.
AI.result: Method benchmarked on single-qubit X gate, leakage-prone qutrit task, and two-qubit entangling gate. Not universally best in fidelity or computational cost, but exposes low-complexity frontier. Qutrit fidelity: 0.6672±0.0001, two-qubit: 0.6342±0.0003 with lower complexity than unconstrained solutions.
AI.conclusion: PADMM serves as a constraint-native framework for exploring low-complexity frontiers in quantum control, not as a replacement for unconstrained high-fidelity solvers. Training-time robust optimization provides task-dependent gains, with clearest effect in qutrit drift robustness.

title: Floquet Dissipative Phase Transitions
summary: Dissipative phase transitions (DPTs) are traditionally characterized through the spectral properties of a time-independent Liouvillian superoperator. However, this definition cannot be applied to time-periodic (Floquet) systems that cannot be exactly recast into equivalent time-independent problems. In this article, we develop a general framework to characterize DPTs in time-periodic open quantum systems by analyzing the spectrum of the Floquet propagator. We first study driven-dissipative Kerr resonators, known to display a DPT, showing that counter-rotating terms in the drive induce a shift in the critical point and a significant change in the time scales associated with the transition. We then investigate DPTs in the driven quantum Rabi model and in its time-independent approximated counterpart, the driven Jaynes-Cummings model. We find that the Rabi model exhibits distinct critical features as the ultrastrong coupling regime is approached. Moreover, our Floquet analysis unveils the disappearance of the DPT in the deep strong coupling regime of the quantum Rabi model due to light-matter decoupling. Our rigorous approach sets the stage for the study of dissipative criticality in a broad class of time-dependent open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a Floquet framework to characterize dissipative phase transitions in time-periodic open quantum systems, overcoming limitations of traditional time-independent Liouvillian approaches.
AI.motivation: Traditional characterization of dissipative phase transitions using time-independent Liouvillian superoperators cannot be applied to time-periodic (Floquet) systems that lack exact time-independent equivalents, creating a gap in understanding critical phenomena in driven-dissipative quantum systems.
AI.method: Develops a general framework using Floquet propagator spectrum analysis to characterize DPTs in time-periodic open quantum systems. Applies this to driven-dissipative Kerr resonators, driven quantum Rabi model, and its Jaynes-Cummings approximation.
AI.result: Counter-rotating terms in driven-dissipative Kerr resonators shift critical points and alter transition time scales. The Rabi model shows distinct critical features approaching ultrastrong coupling, with DPT disappearance in deep strong coupling regime due to light-matter decoupling.
AI.conclusion: The Floquet framework enables rigorous study of dissipative criticality in time-dependent open quantum systems, revealing new phenomena like critical point shifts, altered dynamics, and DPT disappearance in strong coupling regimes.

title: Noise mitigation of quantum observables via learning from Hamiltonian symmetry decays
summary: We present a new quantum error mitigation technique (QEM), called GUiding Extrapolations from Symmetry decayS (GUESS), which exploits Hamiltonian symmetries to improve accuracy of noisy quantum computations. This method is explicitly designed for quantum algorithms that estimate expectation values of observables and consists in learning the extrapolation coefficients from a symmetry observable of the system to then estimate the value of a target observable. Furthermore, we propose a Hamiltonian impurity technique to enforce symmetries allowing the mitigation of local observables of interest. We employ the IBM Heron r2 quantum processing unit '\texttt{ibm\_basquecountry}' to simulate the time evolution of average magnetization and nearest-neighbor correlator observables for transverse field Ising and $XZ$ Heisenberg models in 1D with open boundary conditions. We benchmark the accuracy of our method against baseline Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) and tensor network simulations for systems of $100$ qubits. Remarkably, GUESS achieves a relative error around $10\%$ for circuits containing up to $8000$ CZ gates, while showcasing lower variance than ZNE on average across $20$ observables and requiring only twice the number of shots per observable compared to baseline ZNE. Furthermore, we demonstrate that GUESS enables statistical post-selection based on the outcomes of the symmetry observable, which provides critical information about the quality of the target qubits by means of its mean and variance. These results indicate that GUESS is a powerful QEM technique capable of mitigating utility-scale circuit outcomes, delivering high accuracy and reduced variance for large-scale circuits with minimal quantum overhead.

AI.tldr: GUESS is a quantum error mitigation technique that uses Hamiltonian symmetries to improve expectation value estimation, achieving ~10% relative error for 100-qubit systems with up to 8000 CZ gates while requiring only twice the shots of baseline ZNE.
AI.motivation: Current quantum error mitigation techniques like Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) have limitations in accuracy and variance for large-scale quantum computations. There's a need for methods that can handle utility-scale circuits with minimal quantum overhead while providing reliable error mitigation for expectation values of observables.
AI.method: GUESS exploits Hamiltonian symmetries by learning extrapolation coefficients from a symmetry observable to estimate target observables. It includes a Hamiltonian impurity technique to enforce symmetries for local observables. The method was tested on IBM Heron r2 quantum hardware simulating time evolution of transverse field Ising and XZ Heisenberg models in 1D with open boundary conditions, benchmarking against ZNE and tensor network simulations for 100-qubit systems.
AI.result: GUESS achieves ~10% relative error for circuits with up to 8000 CZ gates, shows lower variance than ZNE across 20 observables, requires only twice the shots per observable compared to baseline ZNE, and enables statistical post-selection based on symmetry observable outcomes to assess qubit quality.
AI.conclusion: GUESS is a powerful quantum error mitigation technique capable of mitigating utility-scale circuit outcomes with high accuracy, reduced variance, and minimal quantum overhead, making it suitable for large-scale quantum computations.

title: Practical framework for simulating permutation-equivariant quantum circuits
summary: Understanding which subclasses of quantum circuits are efficiently classically simulable is fundamental to delineating the boundary between classical and quantum computation. In this context, it is well known that certain tasks based on permutation-equivariant unitaries-i.e., $n$-qubit circuits whose action commutes with the qubit-permuting representation of the symmetric group $S_n$-can be simulated in polynomial time. However, existing approaches scale as $O(n^7)$, and can rapidly become prohibitively expensive. In this work, we introduce a practical algorithm for simulating $S_n$-equivariant circuits under the assumption that the gate generators are at most $k$-local, with $k\in O(1)$. The resulting method runs in $O(n^{ω+1})$ time for constant depth, where $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent, significantly lowering the polynomial degree compared to existing techniques. Finally, we numerically validate this scaling by simulating the dynamical evolution of the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, and show that for $n=512$ spins, a standard laptop can compute the concurrence of the evolved state in under two minutes.

AI.tldr: A practical algorithm for simulating symmetric quantum circuits that runs in O(n^{ω+1}) time, significantly faster than existing O(n^7) methods.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for simulating permutation-equivariant quantum circuits scale as O(n^7), which becomes prohibitively expensive for large systems. There's a need for more efficient classical simulation algorithms to better understand the boundary between classical and quantum computation.
AI.method: Introduces a practical algorithm for simulating S_n-equivariant circuits under the assumption that gate generators are at most k-local with k∈O(1). The method exploits symmetry properties and runs in O(n^{ω+1}) time for constant depth circuits, where ω is the matrix multiplication exponent.
AI.result: The algorithm significantly reduces the polynomial degree compared to existing techniques (from O(n^7) to O(n^{ω+1})). Numerical validation shows that for n=512 spins, a standard laptop can compute the concurrence of the evolved state in under two minutes when simulating the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm provides a practical and significantly more efficient method for simulating symmetric quantum circuits, enabling classical simulation of larger quantum systems than previously possible with existing techniques.

title: Exponential Scaling Barriers for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
comment: 11 pages and 6 figures in the main article
summary: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is widely regarded as a promising algorithm for calculating ground states of quantum systems that are intractable for classical computers. This promise is typically motivated by the hope of mitigating the exponential growth of Hilbert space with system size. Here we scrutinize how the computational cost of adaptive VQE scales with the size of the target system. We demonstrate that the Rényi entropy derived from classical simulations predicts the required number of adaptive iterations of VQE with high accuracy ($R^2 \approx 0.99$). We validate this on a benchmarking set of more than 20 different molecules with active spaces ranging from four to ten orbitals. For these molecules, we find an exponential scaling of the number of adaptive iterations, and in turn, of the circuit depth with the system size. We therefore conclude that it is unlikely that VQE in its current form is able to simulate large molecular systems with high fidelity without exponential resource requirements.

AI.tldr: VQE's computational cost scales exponentially with system size, as predicted by Rényi entropy from classical simulations, challenging its viability for large quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To scrutinize how the computational cost of adaptive Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) scales with the size of target quantum systems, particularly examining whether VQE can truly mitigate the exponential growth of Hilbert space.
AI.method: Used classical simulations to derive Rényi entropy as a predictor for required adaptive VQE iterations, validated on a benchmarking set of more than 20 different molecules with active spaces ranging from 4 to 10 orbitals.
AI.result: Rényi entropy accurately predicts required adaptive VQE iterations (R² ≈ 0.99). For the tested molecules, found exponential scaling of both adaptive iterations and circuit depth with system size.
AI.conclusion: VQE in its current form is unlikely to simulate large molecular systems with high fidelity without exponential resource requirements, challenging its promise for quantum advantage.

title: Is the matrix completion of reduced density matrices unique?
summary: Reduced density matrices are central to describing observables in many-body quantum systems. In electronic structure theory, the two-particle reduced density matrix (2-RDM) suffices to determine the energy and other key properties. Recent work has used matrix completion, leveraging the low-rank structure of RDMs and approximate theoretical models, to reconstruct the 2-RDM from partial data and thus reduce computational cost. However, matrix completion is, in general, an under-determined problem. Revisiting Rosina's theorem [M. Rosina, Queen's Papers on Pure and Applied Mathematics No. 11, 369 (1968)], we here show that the matrix completion is unique under certain conditions, identifying the subset of 2-RDM elements that enables its exact reconstruction from incomplete information. Building on this, we introduce a hybrid quantum-stochastic algorithm that achieves exact matrix completion, demonstrated through applications to the Fermi-Hubbard model.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes uniqueness conditions for 2-RDM matrix completion via Rosina's theorem and introduces a hybrid quantum-stochastic algorithm for exact reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Matrix completion for 2-RDMs is generally under-determined, creating ambiguity in reconstruction from partial data. The work aims to identify conditions under which unique completion is possible and develop practical algorithms leveraging this theoretical foundation.
AI.method: Revisits Rosina's theorem to establish uniqueness conditions for 2-RDM matrix completion, then develops a hybrid quantum-stochastic algorithm that combines quantum computing with stochastic methods to achieve exact reconstruction.
AI.result: Identifies specific subsets of 2-RDM elements that enable exact reconstruction from incomplete information. Demonstrates successful application to the Fermi-Hubbard model using the proposed hybrid algorithm.
AI.conclusion: Theoretical uniqueness conditions enable exact 2-RDM matrix completion, and the hybrid quantum-stochastic algorithm provides a practical implementation, reducing computational costs while maintaining accuracy for quantum many-body systems.

title: Trajectory-independent speed limits for controlled open quantum systems
summary: Existing quantum speed limits for controlled open quantum systems depend on the specified trajectory. For example, lower bounds on quantum annealing times in the presence of dissipation depend explicitly on the chosen annealing schedule. Recently, schedule-independent speed limits have been derived for annealing in the closed quantum system setting (SciPost Phys. 18, 159 (2025)). In this work, we generalize these results to open quantum systems, deriving schedule-independent lower bounds for quantum annealing times in systems described by a Lindblad master equation. We analyze the interplay between coherent control and dissipation in single- and two-qubit examples, demonstrating that the derived lower bounds capture key scaling behavior with respect to the strength of the dissipator. Finally, we apply the bound to thermal state preparation and show that the bound matches the expected asymptotic behavior for an Ising model in the high temperature limit.

AI.tldr: Schedule-independent quantum speed limits for annealing in open quantum systems described by Lindblad master equations, generalizing previous closed-system results.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum speed limits for controlled open quantum systems depend on the specific trajectory/annealing schedule, limiting their general applicability. Recent schedule-independent bounds for closed systems need extension to open quantum systems.
AI.method: Generalize schedule-independent speed limits to open quantum systems described by Lindblad master equations. Derive lower bounds for quantum annealing times that are independent of the specific annealing schedule. Analyze single- and two-qubit examples to study coherent control-dissipation interplay.
AI.result: Derived schedule-independent lower bounds for quantum annealing times in open quantum systems. Demonstrated that bounds capture key scaling behavior with respect to dissipator strength. Applied bound to thermal state preparation showing matching asymptotic behavior for Ising model in high temperature limit.
AI.conclusion: Successfully generalized schedule-independent quantum speed limits to open quantum systems, providing bounds that capture essential scaling behavior and apply to practical scenarios like thermal state preparation.

title: Partially Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation for Megaquop Applications
summary: Partially fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) has recently emerged as a promising approach for the execution of megaquop-scale circuits with millions of logical operations. In this work, we demonstrate the strengths and the limitations of this approach by conducting quantum resource estimation (QRE) of the space--time-efficient analog rotation (STAR) architecture using realistic hardware specifications for superconducting processors, and compare it against the QRE of the full FTQC architecture. We show how the performance of the STAR architecture's protocols is affected by hardware improvements. We also reduce the space requirements for partial FTQC by developing a procedure leveraging code growth to decrease the size of a factory producing analog rotation states. Our results reveal a non-trivial dependence of the optimal pre-growth code distance on the rotation angle with respect to post-growth infidelity. Further, we analyze space--time trade-offs between the factory size and the error-mitigation overhead, and observe that in an application-agnostic setting, there is a Goldilocks zone for circuits in the regime of roughly $10^5$--$10^6$ small-angle rotation gates. We show that quantum simulation of 2D Fermi--Hubbard model systems is a particularly well-suited application for the STAR architecture, requiring only hundreds of thousands of physical qubits and runtimes on the order of minutes for modest system sizes. Due to its favourable algorithmic scaling to larger system sizes, utility-scale simulation of the 2D Fermi--Hubbard model could potentially be attained using partial FTQC.

AI.tldr: Partial FTQC enables megaquop-scale quantum circuits; STAR architecture shows optimal performance for 10^5-10^6 small-angle rotations, with Fermi-Hubbard simulations requiring only hundreds of thousands of qubits.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the practical potential of partially fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) as an intermediate approach between NISQ and full FTQC, specifically assessing the STAR architecture's performance with realistic superconducting hardware constraints.
AI.method: Conducted quantum resource estimation (QRE) comparing STAR architecture against full FTQC using realistic superconducting processor specifications; developed code growth procedure to reduce factory size for analog rotation states; analyzed space-time trade-offs and optimal pre-growth code distances.
AI.result: STAR architecture shows non-trivial dependence of optimal pre-growth code distance on rotation angle; identifies Goldilocks zone for circuits with 10^5-10^6 small-angle rotations; Fermi-Hubbard simulations require only hundreds of thousands of physical qubits with minute-scale runtimes; partial FTQC enables utility-scale simulations.
AI.conclusion: Partially fault-tolerant quantum computing via STAR architecture offers a practical pathway to megaquop-scale quantum advantage, particularly well-suited for quantum simulation applications like the 2D Fermi-Hubbard model, bridging the gap between NISQ and full FTQC capabilities.

title: Experimental realization of a $\cos(2\varphi)$ transmon qubit
summary: Superconducting circuits with embedded symmetries are good candidates to robustly protect quantum information from dominant error channels. The $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit, consisting of an island shunted to ground through a tunneling element that selectively transmits pairs of Cooper pairs, leverages charge-parity symmetry to protect from charge-induced errors. In this experiment, we observe a doublet of states of opposite Cooper-pair parity split by $13.6~\mathrm{MHz}$. Operating in a soft-transmon regime, this splitting is two orders of magnitude smaller than in previous implementations, pushing charge-induced losses well beyond the measured coherence times. Despite the low transition frequency, we demonstrate coherent qubit control, single-shot readout, and resolve quantum jumps. Charge protection of the qubit is evidenced by a $100-$fold suppression of the island charge matrix element compared to the unprotected plasmon transition, placing dielectric loss limits above $10~\mathrm{ms}$. The measured $T_1 = 70~μ\mathrm{s}$ and $T_2^\mathrm{echo}= 2.5~μ\mathrm{s}$ are instead limited by $1/f$ flux noise in the tunnelling element's loop. This experiment shows that pushing Cooper-pair pairing in the transmon regime sets high limits on charge-induced losses while preserving coherent control and single-shot readout of the low-frequency qubit. We identify flux noise as the dominant remaining limitation, calling for gradiometric designs or novel $4e$-tunneling elements.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of a cos(2φ) qubit in soft-transmon regime showing enhanced charge protection, coherent control, and single-shot readout despite low transition frequency, with flux noise identified as main limitation.
AI.motivation: To develop superconducting qubits with embedded symmetries that robustly protect quantum information from dominant error channels, specifically addressing charge-induced errors through charge-parity symmetry protection.
AI.method: Implemented a cos(2φ) qubit consisting of an island shunted to ground through a tunneling element that selectively transmits pairs of Cooper pairs, operating in a soft-transmon regime to achieve two orders of magnitude smaller parity splitting than previous implementations.
AI.result: Observed doublet of states with opposite Cooper-pair parity split by 13.6 MHz, demonstrated coherent qubit control, single-shot readout, and resolved quantum jumps. Achieved 100-fold suppression of island charge matrix element compared to unprotected plasmon transition, with T₁ = 70 μs and T₂^echo = 2.5 μs limited by 1/f flux noise.
AI.conclusion: Pushing Cooper-pair pairing into the transmon regime sets high limits on charge-induced losses while preserving coherent control and single-shot readout, with flux noise identified as the dominant remaining limitation requiring gradiometric designs or novel 4e-tunneling elements.

title: On-Demand Correlated Errors in Superconducting Qubits from a Particle Accelerator
summary: Ionizing radiation is a known source of correlated errors in superconducting quantum processors, inhibiting the functionality of quantum error correction surface codes. High-energy photons and charged particles deposit pair-breaking energy into these systems leading to excess quasiparticles near Josephson junctions that increase qubit decoherence. Previous investigations of this problem have relied on ambient, stochastic sources of ionizing radiation or alternative methods of quasiparticle generation. Here, we present a facility that couples an electron linear accelerator (linac) to a dilution refrigerator to study ionizing radiation in quantum systems. A single linac electron closely mimics the energy deposition characteristics of a typical cosmic-ray muon, and we demonstrate the facility's usefulness with a multi-qubit superconducting transmon chip. Characteristic radiation-induced relaxation errors are quickly and easily collected with the speed and timing information of the linac. Additionally, we present qubit excitation and detuning errors that can be difficult to detect without the on-demand source of ionizing radiation. These error signatures are shown to be dependent on the junction placement and surrounding superconducting gaps.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed a facility combining an electron linear accelerator with a dilution refrigerator to study ionizing radiation effects on superconducting quantum processors, enabling controlled experiments that mimic cosmic-ray muon impacts and revealing various radiation-induced error signatures in transmon qubits.
AI.motivation: Ionizing radiation causes correlated errors in superconducting quantum processors that inhibit quantum error correction surface codes. Previous studies relied on stochastic ambient radiation or indirect quasiparticle generation methods, lacking controlled, on-demand radiation sources for systematic investigation.
AI.method: Developed a facility coupling an electron linear accelerator (linac) to a dilution refrigerator. Used single linac electrons to mimic cosmic-ray muon energy deposition characteristics. Tested with multi-qubit superconducting transmon chip, leveraging the linac's speed and timing information for efficient data collection.
AI.result: Successfully collected characteristic radiation-induced relaxation errors quickly using linac timing. Detected qubit excitation and detuning errors that are difficult to observe without on-demand radiation sources. Found error signatures depend on junction placement and surrounding superconducting gaps.
AI.conclusion: The linac-coupled facility provides a powerful tool for studying ionizing radiation effects in quantum systems, enabling controlled experiments that reveal previously hard-to-detect error signatures and their dependence on device geometry, which is crucial for developing radiation-hardened quantum processors.

title: Universal monitored dynamics in multimode bosonic systems
summary: We propose a route to study monitored many-body dynamics in multimode bosonic systems using circuit quantum electrodynamics. In this experimental setting, we construct several bosonic models comprising brickwork circuits built from beam-splitter gates, local parity measurements, and optional on-site Hubbard interactions, and diagnose their monitored dynamics via ancilla purification and a learnability-based probe. Under parity measurements, generic gate sets exhibit behavior that is largely consistent with a conventional measurement-induced phase transition, while a special class of beam-splitter circuits shows an apparent critical-like high-measurement regime in which purification times scale linearly with system size. We show that for realistic noise, gate, and measurement rates, these signatures are observable with near-term circuit QED hardware.

AI.tldr: Experimental proposal for studying monitored many-body dynamics in bosonic systems using circuit QED, showing measurement-induced phase transitions with linear purification scaling in special beam-splitter circuits.
AI.motivation: To investigate monitored many-body dynamics in bosonic systems using circuit quantum electrodynamics as an experimental platform, focusing on measurement-induced phase transitions that are challenging to study in conventional settings.
AI.method: Construct bosonic models using brickwork circuits built from beam-splitter gates, local parity measurements, and optional Hubbard interactions. Diagnose dynamics via ancilla purification and learnability-based probes in circuit QED hardware.
AI.result: Generic gate sets show conventional measurement-induced phase transitions, while special beam-splitter circuits exhibit critical-like high-measurement regime with purification times scaling linearly with system size. These signatures are observable with near-term circuit QED hardware under realistic noise and measurement rates.
AI.conclusion: Circuit QED provides a viable experimental platform for studying monitored many-body dynamics and measurement-induced phase transitions in bosonic systems, with observable signatures in near-term hardware.

title: Extracting information from a superradiant burst using simple measurements
summary: It is well known that superradiant decay of an ensemble of $N$ spins generates a complex non-classical state of light. Here, we consider the information content of a superradiant burst of photons: how is information encoded in the initial spin state distributed among the emitted photons, and can it be extracted using simple measurements? Despite the complexity of the photonic burst state, we show that a simple homodyne measurement combined with an optimized filter and linear estimator recovers the $N$-scaling of the quantum Fisher information of the initial spin state (including cases exhibiting $N^2$ Heisenberg scaling). Even more surprising, the temporal mode with optimal information content contains a vanishing fraction of the total emitted photons in the large-$N$ limit, suggesting an effective compressing of information. Our results and setup represent a new way to perform cavity based readout of solid-state spin ensembles that allows one to utilize resonant spin-photon interactions.

AI.tldr: Superradiant bursts encode spin state information in photons; optimal information extraction uses homodyne measurement with optimized filtering, achieving quantum Fisher information scaling despite minimal photon fraction.
AI.motivation: To understand how information from an initial spin state is distributed among photons in superradiant decay and whether it can be extracted with simple measurements, particularly for cavity-based readout of solid-state spin ensembles.
AI.method: Analyze superradiant photon bursts using homodyne measurement combined with optimized temporal filtering and linear estimation to extract spin state information.
AI.result: Simple homodyne measurement with optimized filter recovers N-scaling of quantum Fisher information (including Heisenberg N² scaling). Optimal temporal mode contains vanishing fraction of total emitted photons at large N, indicating information compression.
AI.conclusion: Superradiant bursts effectively encode spin information in photons, enabling efficient cavity-based readout of solid-state spin ensembles using resonant spin-photon interactions with simple measurement techniques.

title: Asymptotic non-Hermitian degeneracy phenomenon and its exactly solvable simulation
summary: Up to these days, the popular PT-symmetric imaginary cubic oscillator did not find any consistent probabilistic quantum-mechanical interpretation because its Hamiltonian has been shown, by mathematicians, intrinsic-exceptional-point (IEP) singular. In the paper we explain why there is even no reasonable small-perturbation-based regularization of the similar unacceptable (i.e., IEP-singular) quantum models. The explanation is based on a partial formal analogy of the IEP singularity with the conventional exceptional point (EP). What is important is that we are able to construct a simplified $N$ by $N$-matrix (and exactly solvable) toy-model Hamiltonian admitting the asymptotic (i.e., high-excitation) EP-related wave-function degeneracy which, in some sense (i.e., in the limit of large $N$) mimics several aspects of its IEP analogue. In this comparison, the difference is that the regularization of the EP singularities is possible (using an ad hoc perturbation of size ${\cal O}(1/N)$) while an analogous regularization of the IEP singularity is not (we have to consider $N \to \infty$).

AI.tldr: The paper explains why PT-symmetric imaginary cubic oscillators lack consistent quantum interpretation due to intrinsic-exceptional-point singularities, and shows that while EP singularities can be regularized, IEP singularities cannot.
AI.motivation: To understand why PT-symmetric imaginary cubic oscillators have no consistent probabilistic quantum-mechanical interpretation and why their IEP singularities cannot be regularized via small perturbations.
AI.method: Constructs a simplified N×N exactly solvable matrix toy-model Hamiltonian that asymptotically mimics IEP behavior, comparing EP and IEP regularization possibilities through perturbation analysis.
AI.result: EP singularities can be regularized with O(1/N) perturbations, but IEP singularities cannot be regularized even in the N→∞ limit, explaining the fundamental interpretational problem.
AI.conclusion: The intrinsic-exceptional-point singularity of PT-symmetric imaginary cubic oscillators represents a fundamental obstruction to consistent quantum interpretation that cannot be resolved through perturbation regularization.

title: Robustness and optimization of N00N-state interferometry
summary: Quantum-enhanced interferometry is often discussed in terms of ideal resources and asymptotic scalings, whereas in practice its performance is set by a delicate interplay between losses, state imbalance, and photon number. We address this interplay in a folded Franson interferometer fed with partially entangled N00N states, treating asymmetric losses and tunable input imbalance on equal footing. From exact detection probabilities we obtain closed-form expressions for the fringe visibility and the Fisher information, and show that these two figures of merit respond very differently to imperfections. In particular, we demonstrate that perfect interference contrast can always be recovered by compensating loss asymmetry with an appropriate input imbalance, while the Fisher information generally peaks at a distinct operating point, reflecting the irreducible trade-off between coherence restoration and signal attenuation. By determining the exact optima and benchmarking against single-photon strategies, we identify the critical loss and minimum entanglement required to maintain a genuine quantum advantage over optimized single-photon strategies under identical loss conditions, and establish their scaling with the photon number N . Beyond delineating the fundamental trade-offs between loss, entanglement, and sensitivity, this work establishes a comprehensive theoretical framework that both underpins and extends the experimental demonstration of quantum advantage reported in [1], providing a unified description of the relevant operating regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes quantum-enhanced interferometry with partially entangled N00N states in a folded Franson interferometer, examining how losses, state imbalance, and photon number interact to affect performance metrics like fringe visibility and Fisher information.
AI.motivation: Quantum-enhanced interferometry is typically discussed in ideal terms with asymptotic scalings, but practical performance depends on the delicate interplay between losses, state imbalance, and photon number. The authors aim to address this practical reality by treating asymmetric losses and tunable input imbalance on equal footing.
AI.method: The authors use a folded Franson interferometer fed with partially entangled N00N states. They derive exact detection probabilities from which they obtain closed-form expressions for fringe visibility and Fisher information. They analyze how these metrics respond to imperfections and determine optimal operating points.
AI.result: The study shows that fringe visibility and Fisher information respond differently to imperfections: perfect interference contrast can always be recovered by compensating loss asymmetry with appropriate input imbalance, while Fisher information generally peaks at a distinct operating point. The authors identify critical loss thresholds and minimum entanglement requirements for maintaining quantum advantage over optimized single-photon strategies, and establish their scaling with photon number N.
AI.conclusion: The work delineates fundamental trade-offs between loss, entanglement, and sensitivity in quantum-enhanced interferometry. It establishes a comprehensive theoretical framework that both underpins and extends experimental demonstrations of quantum advantage, providing a unified description of relevant operating regimes for practical quantum metrology.

title: Accessing which-path information in the absorption and emission of light by a quantum dot in a Ramsey sequence
summary: We quantify which-path information in the absorption and emission of light by a quantum dot along a Ramsey-like sequence. The quantum dot is excited by two successive classical $π/2$-pulses with tunable relative phase, yielding the spontaneous release of coherent superpositions of zero- and one-photon Fock states into two successive time bins. Along the sequence, the first time bin extracts information on the quantum dot energy state, behaving as a which-path detector for the Ramsey interferometer. The which-path information increases over time, and is accessed through the reduction of contrast of the Ramsey fringes. After the second pulse, the information still present in the first time bin controls the emission of coherent light into the second time bin, which is measurable through the reduction of the contrast of self-homodyne interference fringes in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Both measurements are in remarkable agreement with theoretical predictions. Our results quantitatively illustrate how which-path information and more generally quantum correlations impact light-matter energy exchanges in the quantum realm.

AI.tldr: Researchers quantify which-path information in quantum dot light absorption/emission using Ramsey-like interferometry, showing how quantum correlations affect light-matter energy exchanges.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively understand how which-path information and quantum correlations impact light-matter energy exchanges in quantum systems, specifically in quantum dot interactions with light.
AI.method: Used a quantum dot excited by two successive classical π/2-pulses with tunable relative phase in a Ramsey-like sequence, creating coherent superpositions of zero- and one-photon Fock states in two time bins. The first time bin acts as a which-path detector, and measurements were made through Ramsey fringe contrast reduction and self-homodyne interference in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer.
AI.result: Experimental measurements show which-path information increases over time and is accessed through reduction of Ramsey fringe contrast. After the second pulse, information in the first time bin controls emission into the second time bin, measurable through self-homodyne interference fringe contrast reduction. Both measurements show remarkable agreement with theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: The study successfully quantifies which-path information in quantum dot light interactions, demonstrating how quantum correlations fundamentally impact light-matter energy exchanges in the quantum realm through controlled interference measurements.

title: Resource-efficient Quantum Algorithms for Selected Hamiltonian Subspace Diagonalization
summary: Quantum algorithms for selecting a subspace of Hamiltonians to diagonalize have emerged as a promising alternative to variational algorithms in the NISQ era. So far, such algorithms, which include the quantum selected configuration interaction (QSCI) and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), have been formulated in second-quantization in Fock space, which leads to inefficient usage of qubit resources. We introduce the first QSCI algorithm developed in the CI-matrix (CIM) framework, which is known to have optimal qubit scaling of exactly $\lceil \log_2 (N_{CSF}) \rceil$ where $N$ is the size of the CIM. In addition, we introduce a novel single-bit flip error mitigation which comes at the overhead of a single qubit and we combine this with a stochastic approximate Trotterization evolution adapted from qDRIFT. Simulating benchmark N$_2$ and naphthalene molecules on quantum hardware, our results achieved similar accuracy as SQD methods but with significantly less quantum resources. However, our CIM-QSCI algorithm and SQD methods could not match the performance of classical heat-bath CI (HCI) for the same task. Hence, we introduce an augmented version of QSCI called quantum selected heat-bath CI (QSHCI). This variant replaces classical heat-bath sampling with quantum sampling from QSCI to achieve performance comparable to HCI. We note that a current drawback of our approach is the preprocessing cost of $\mathcal{O}(N^2\log N)$ for constructing the CIM and performing the Pauli decomposition. This can be further improved by considering efficient CIM access models for the stochastic Trotter evolution.

AI.tldr: First QSCI algorithm in CI-matrix framework with optimal qubit scaling, novel single-bit flip error mitigation, and stochastic Trotterization, achieving similar accuracy as SQD with fewer resources but not matching classical HCI; introduces QSHCI combining quantum sampling with heat-bath CI.
AI.motivation: Quantum subspace diagonalization algorithms (like QSCI and SQD) have been formulated in second-quantization Fock space, leading to inefficient qubit usage. Need to develop quantum algorithms with optimal qubit scaling and better resource efficiency for NISQ-era quantum chemistry.
AI.method: Develops first QSCI algorithm in CI-matrix (CIM) framework with optimal qubit scaling of ⌈log₂(N_CSF)⌉. Introduces novel single-bit flip error mitigation with single-qubit overhead. Combines with stochastic approximate Trotterization adapted from qDRIFT. Simulates benchmark N₂ and naphthalene molecules. Introduces augmented QSHCI variant that replaces classical heat-bath sampling with quantum sampling from QSCI.
AI.result: CIM-QSCI achieved similar accuracy as SQD methods but with significantly less quantum resources. However, neither CIM-QSCI nor SQD could match classical HCI performance. QSHCI variant achieves performance comparable to classical HCI by combining quantum sampling with heat-bath CI approach.
AI.conclusion: CIM framework enables optimal qubit scaling for quantum subspace diagonalization. Novel error mitigation and stochastic Trotterization improve practical implementation. While current methods don't surpass classical HCI, QSHCI hybrid approach shows promise. Main drawback is O(N²logN) preprocessing cost for CIM construction and Pauli decomposition, which could be improved with efficient CIM access models.

title: Circuit Optimization for Universality Transformation
summary: It is known that a computationally universal gate set $\{H,CCZ\}$ can be transformed to a strictly universal one $\{Λ(S), H\}$ using one maximally imaginary state $|+i\rangle$ and non-imaginary ancillary qubits. We succeed this transformation with a shorter circuit that eliminates non-imaginary ancillary qubits. We further extend this to the continuous gate-set setting, showing that any multi-qubit unitary can be exactly generated by real single-qubit unitary gates, $CCZ$ gates and $|+i\rangle$.

AI.tldr: The paper presents circuit optimizations for universal quantum gate sets, eliminating ancillary qubits and extending results to continuous gate sets.
AI.motivation: Previous work showed that the computationally universal gate set {H, CCZ} can be transformed to the strictly universal set {Λ(S), H} using one maximally imaginary state |+i⟩ and non-imaginary ancillary qubits. The authors aim to improve this transformation by reducing circuit complexity and resource requirements.
AI.method: Develops a shorter circuit that eliminates the need for non-imaginary ancillary qubits in the transformation from {H, CCZ} to {Λ(S), H}. Extends this approach to continuous gate sets, showing that any multi-qubit unitary can be exactly generated using real single-qubit unitary gates, CCZ gates, and the |+i⟩ state.
AI.result: Successfully achieves transformation with reduced circuit complexity by eliminating ancillary qubits. Proves that any multi-qubit unitary can be exactly generated by the specified gate set in the continuous setting.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates significant improvements in universal gate set transformations, reducing resource requirements and extending applicability to continuous gate sets, with implications for quantum circuit optimization and resource-efficient quantum computation.

title: Beta Tantalum Transmon Qubits with Quality Factors Approaching 10 Million
summary: Tantalum-based transmon qubits are a promising platform for building large-scale quantum processors. So far, these qubits have been made from tantalum films grown exclusively in the alpha phase (α-Ta). The beta phase of tantalum (\{beta}-Ta) readily nucleates at room temperature, making it attractive for scalable qubit fabrication. However, \{beta}-Ta is widely believed to be detrimental to qubit performance because it has a lower superconducting critical temperature than α-Ta. We challenge this prevailing belief by fabricating low-loss transmon qubits from \{beta}-Ta films on sapphire. Across 11 qubits, the mean time-averaged quality factor is (5.6 +/- 2.3) x 10^6, with the best qubit recording a time-averaged quality factor of (10.1 +/- 1.3) x 10^6. Resonator studies demonstrate that the dominant microwave loss channel is surface two-level systems, with the surface loss contribution for \{beta}-Ta being about twice that of α-Ta. \{beta}-Ta films exhibit significant kinetic inductance, consistent with an estimated magnetic penetration depth of (1.78 +/- 0.02) μm. This work establishes \{beta}-Ta on sapphire as a material platform for realizing low-loss transmon qubits and other superconducting devices such as compact resonators, kinetic inductance detectors, and quasiparticle traps.

AI.tldr: Beta-phase tantalum (β-Ta) transmon qubits achieve high quality factors comparable to alpha-phase Ta, challenging the belief that β-Ta is detrimental to qubit performance.
AI.motivation: Challenge the prevailing belief that β-Ta is detrimental to qubit performance due to its lower superconducting critical temperature compared to α-Ta, and explore β-Ta as an attractive material for scalable qubit fabrication since it readily nucleates at room temperature.
AI.method: Fabricated low-loss transmon qubits from β-Ta films on sapphire substrates, measured 11 qubits to determine time-averaged quality factors, conducted resonator studies to identify microwave loss channels, and characterized kinetic inductance properties.
AI.result: Mean time-averaged quality factor of (5.6 ± 2.3) × 10^6 across 11 qubits, with best qubit achieving (10.1 ± 1.3) × 10^6. Dominant loss channel is surface two-level systems, with β-Ta having about twice the surface loss contribution of α-Ta. β-Ta exhibits significant kinetic inductance with estimated magnetic penetration depth of (1.78 ± 0.02) μm.
AI.conclusion: β-Ta on sapphire is established as a viable material platform for low-loss transmon qubits and other superconducting devices, demonstrating that β-Ta's room-temperature nucleation properties make it attractive for scalable fabrication without sacrificing qubit performance.

title: Fluxon Time-Delay Readout of a Superconducting Qubit Protected by a Spectral Gap in a Josephson Transmission Line
summary: We theoretically investigate a readout scheme of the quantum state of a superconducting qubit based on time delay of a single flux quantum (SFQ), also known as a fluxon, propagating in a Josephson transmission line (JTL). We concretely study the time-delay readout based on capacitive coupling between a transmon qubit and a JTL, and we evaluate the time delay depending on the qubit state. We also reveal a feature of the absence of fluxon pinning and exponential suppression of nonadiabatic transitions caused by the propagating fluxon, which is advantageous for the time-delay readout. We extend the analysis to a multi-level transmon as well. Owing to the spectral gap in the JTL, the radiative decay of the qubit mediated by the JTL is exponentially suppressed, and thus the transmission line itself also serves as a filter protecting the qubit. The readout scheme requires neither complicated wiring to low-temperature stages nor bulky microwave components, which are bottlenecks for integration of a large-scale superconducting quantum computer.

AI.tldr: A theoretical investigation of a superconducting qubit readout scheme using time delay of single flux quantum (fluxon) propagation in a Josephson transmission line, with capacitive coupling to a transmon qubit.
AI.motivation: To develop a simplified readout scheme for superconducting quantum computers that avoids complex wiring and bulky microwave components, which are bottlenecks for large-scale integration.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of time-delay readout based on capacitive coupling between a transmon qubit and a Josephson transmission line (JTL), studying fluxon propagation dynamics and evaluating time delay dependence on qubit state.
AI.result: Time delay depends on qubit state, with advantageous features including absence of fluxon pinning and exponential suppression of nonadiabatic transitions. The JTL's spectral gap exponentially suppresses radiative decay, providing inherent qubit protection.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SFQ-based time-delay readout scheme offers a promising alternative to conventional microwave readout, eliminating complex wiring and bulky components while providing inherent qubit protection through the JTL's filtering properties.

title: Quantifying surface losses in superconducting aluminum microwave resonators
summary: The recent realization of millisecond-scale coherence with tantalum-on-silicon transmon qubits showed that depositing the Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junction in a high purity, ultrahigh vacuum environment was critical for achieving lifetime-limited coherence, motivating careful examination of the aluminum surface two-level system (TLS) bath. Here, we measure the microwave absorption arising from surface TLSs in superconducting aluminum resonators, following methodology developed for tantalum resonators. We vary film and surface properties and correlate microwave measurements with materials characterization. We find that the lifetimes of superconducting aluminum resonators are primarily limited by surface losses associated with TLSs in the 2.7 nm-thick native AlOx. Treatment with 49% HF removes surface AlOx completely; however, rapid oxide regrowth limits improvements in surface loss and long term device stability. Using these measurements we estimate that TLSs in aluminum interfaces contribute around 27% of the relaxation rate of state-of-the-art tantalum-on-silicon qubits that incorporate aluminum-based Josephson junctions.

AI.tldr: Aluminum surface TLSs in native AlOx limit superconducting resonator lifetimes; HF treatment removes oxide but regrowth limits improvements; TLSs contribute ~27% to state-of-the-art Ta-on-Si qubit relaxation rates.
AI.motivation: Recent millisecond-scale coherence in tantalum-on-silicon transmon qubits showed that high-purity Josephson junction deposition is critical for lifetime-limited coherence, motivating examination of aluminum surface two-level system (TLS) bath that could limit performance.
AI.method: Measure microwave absorption from surface TLSs in superconducting aluminum resonators using methodology developed for tantalum resonators. Vary film and surface properties, correlate microwave measurements with materials characterization. Treat surfaces with 49% HF to remove native AlOx.
AI.result: Superconducting aluminum resonator lifetimes are primarily limited by surface losses from TLSs in the 2.7 nm-thick native AlOx. HF treatment completely removes surface AlOx, but rapid oxide regrowth limits improvements in surface loss and long-term device stability.
AI.conclusion: TLSs in aluminum interfaces contribute approximately 27% of the relaxation rate of state-of-the-art tantalum-on-silicon qubits that incorporate aluminum-based Josephson junctions, highlighting the importance of surface oxide management for quantum device performance.

title: CANOE: Classically Assisted Non-Orthogonal Eigensolver
summary: In the early fault-tolerant regime, where quantum resources remain limited, hybrid quantum-classical strategies offer one possible route toward quantum advantage. We introduce CANOE, the Classically Assisted Non-Orthogonal Eigensolver, as such an approach, distributing Rayleigh-Ritz basis states between quantum and classical hardware. This approach leverages the expressive power of quantum states, which are costly to reproduce classically, while augmenting them with a large pool of classically generated basis states that can be incorporated at negligible computational cost. We validate this through numerical simulations of a 76-qubit chromium atom system, quantifying how each additional quantum basis state enhances ground-state representability and how the inclusion of classical states further amplifies this improvement.
